DEATH OF A PARTY WHILE A TERMINATION CLAIM IS ALIVE: SURVIVAL OF THE CAUSE OF ACTION, WHO MAY PROSECUTE IT, AND THE DAMAGES THAT REMAIN (CODE CIV. PROC. §§ 366.1, 377.11, 377.20, 377.21, 377.30-377.34, 377.40, 377.41; PROB. CODE §§ 9351, 9370; COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES V. SUPERIOR COURT; RUBIO V. CIA WHEEL GROUP; QUIROZ V. SEVENTH AVENUE CENTER; PRILLIMAN V. UNITED AIR LINES) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Maria Delgado

WHAT THIS SHEET COVERS
Every other document in this corpus about the end of employment assumes that the former employee is alive to pursue whatever the separation left behind, and that the employer still exists to answer for it. This sheet describes what California statutes and published California opinions say happens when that assumption fails and a party dies while a termination-related claim is alive — a wrongful-termination action, a discrimination or retaliation claim, a suit for unpaid final wages, or an administrative matter that has become a lawsuit. The corpus already covers the money a deceased employee leaves behind: the affidavit procedure by which a surviving spouse collects a decedent's unpaid compensation without probate, the COBRA and Cal-COBRA qualifying event that the covered employee's death creates, and the group life insurance conversion privilege. It has not previously covered the claim itself. The sheet sets out the survival statutes in the Code of Civil Procedure (Chapter 4 of Title 3 of Part 2, "Effect of Death"): whether the cause of action is lost, who takes it, what must be filed to prosecute or continue it, how long there is to start it, what damages remain recoverable and what damages drop out, and the mirror-image rules that apply when it is the employer who dies. It states what the authorities say. It does not evaluate the position of Maria Delgado, of Luis Delgado, or of Northgate Components, Inc., and it does not say what any of them should do.

SECTIONS 377.20 AND 377.21: THE CAUSE OF ACTION IS NOT LOST, AND A PENDING CASE DOES NOT ABATE
Code of Civil Procedure section 377.20 states the general rule of survival. Subdivision (a) provides that, except as otherwise provided by statute, a cause of action for or against a person is not lost by reason of the person's death, but survives subject to the applicable limitations period. Subdivision (b) adds that the section applies even where the loss or damage occurs simultaneously with, or after, the death of the person who would have been liable. Section 377.21 states the companion rule for a case already on file: a pending action or proceeding does not abate by the death of a party if the cause of action survives. The two sections sit in Article 2 of the chapter, headed "Survival and Continuation." Read together they set the default in California: death changes who prosecutes or defends a claim arising out of the end of employment of Maria Delgado, and it changes what damages are recoverable, but it does not by itself extinguish the claim or end the lawsuit.

SECTIONS 377.30 AND 377.11: THE CLAIM PASSES TO THE SUCCESSOR IN INTEREST
Section 377.30 provides that a cause of action that survives the death of the person entitled to commence an action passes to the decedent's successor in interest, subject to the Probate Code chapter beginning at section 7000, and that an action may be commenced by the decedent's personal representative or, if none, by the decedent's successor in interest. The order matters on the face of the statute: the personal representative first, the successor in interest only if there is none. Section 377.11 supplies the definition used throughout the chapter — a "decedent's successor in interest" is the beneficiary of the decedent's estate or other successor in interest who succeeds to a cause of action or to a particular item of the property that is the subject of a cause of action. On the face of these two sections, a claim of Maria Delgado arising out of the separation is prosecuted after death by a person occupying one of those two statutory roles, and not by an heir simply because the heir is an heir.

SECTIONS 377.31 AND 377.33: CONTINUING A CASE THAT WAS ALREADY ON FILE
Where the employee died after filing, section 377.31 governs. On motion after the death of a person who commenced an action or proceeding, the court shall allow a pending action or proceeding that does not abate to be continued by the decedent's personal representative or, if none, by the decedent's successor in interest. The verb is "shall," and the trigger is a motion; the statute does not make continuation automatic on the filing of a notice of death, and it does not make it discretionary once the conditions are met. Section 377.33 gives the court authority over the shape of the case that results: the court in which an action is commenced or continued under the article may make any order concerning parties that is appropriate to ensure proper administration of justice, including appointment of the decedent's successor in interest as a special administrator or guardian ad litem.

SECTION 377.32: THE DECLARATION THE SUCCESSOR IN INTEREST MUST FILE
Section 377.32 states what a person proceeding as the decedent's successor in interest must put on file. Subdivision (a) requires an affidavit or a declaration under penalty of perjury under the laws of this state stating all of seven listed items: the decedent's name; the date and place of the decedent's death; the statement "No proceeding is now pending in California for administration of the decedent's estate"; if the estate was administered, a copy of the final order showing distribution of the cause of action to the successor in interest; one of two alternative statements, with supporting facts, that the declarant either is the decedent's successor in interest as defined in section 377.11 or is authorized to act on that person's behalf; the statement that no other person has a superior right to commence the action or to be substituted for the decedent; and the affirmation under penalty of perjury. Subdivision (b) provides that where more than one person executes the declaration, the required statements are modified as appropriate. Subdivision (c) requires that a certified copy of the decedent's death certificate be attached. Several of the required statements are set out in the statute in quotation marks as fixed wording rather than described in substance.

SECTION 366.1: THE SIX-MONTH EXTENSION AFTER DEATH
Section 366.1 addresses timing. If a person entitled to bring an action dies before the expiration of the applicable limitations period, and the cause of action survives, an action may be commenced before the expiration of the later of two times: six months after the person's death, or the limitations period that would have been applicable if the person had not died. The section operates as a floor rather than a substitute: it does not shorten a limitations period that still has more than six months to run, and it does not revive one that had already expired before the death, because it applies only where the person died "before the expiration of the applicable limitations period." Whatever deadline applied to a claim of Maria Delgado arising out of the separation — the wage-claim periods, the Fair Employment and Housing Act periods, the general tort period — is the period the section measures against.

SECTION 377.34, SUBDIVISION (A): PENALTIES AND PUNITIVE DAMAGES SURVIVE; PAIN AND SUFFERING DOES NOT
Section 377.34, subdivision (a), is the damages rule for a survival action. In an action or proceeding by a decedent's personal representative or successor in interest on the decedent's cause of action, the damages recoverable are limited to the loss or damage that the decedent sustained or incurred before death, including any penalties or punitive or exemplary damages that the decedent would have been entitled to recover had the decedent lived, and do not include damages for pain, suffering, or disfigurement. Three features of that sentence bear directly on a termination claim. Damages are cut off at the date of death, so post-death losses are outside the subdivision. Statutory penalties are expressly included, which on the face of the text covers the penalty provisions that run through the wage statutes. Punitive or exemplary damages are expressly included. What the subdivision removes is the category that in a discharge case is often the largest: damages for pain, suffering, or disfigurement, which is where emotional-distress damages sit.

SECTION 377.34, SUBDIVISIONS (B) THROUGH (D): A WINDOW THAT CLOSED ON JANUARY 1, 2026
Subdivision (b) of section 377.34, added by Senate Bill 447 (Stats. 2021, Ch. 448), suspended the pain-and-suffering bar for a defined set of cases. Notwithstanding subdivision (a), the damages recoverable may include damages for pain, suffering, or disfigurement if the action or proceeding was granted a preference pursuant to section 36 before January 1, 2022, or was filed on or after January 1, 2022, and before January 1, 2026. The window is defined by filing date, not by date of death and not by trial date. Subdivision (c) requires a plaintiff who recovers damages pursuant to subdivision (b) between January 1, 2022, and January 1, 2025, inclusive, to submit specified material to the Judicial Council within 60 days of judgment, consent judgment or court-approved settlement. Subdivision (d)(1) required the Judicial Council, on or before January 1, 2025, to transmit a report to the Legislature covering dispositions from January 1, 2022, to July 31, 2024. On the date this sheet was checked, the Legislative Counsel's history note for the section records its most recent amendment as Stats. 2023, Ch. 131, Sec. 18 (AB 1754), effective January 1, 2024, and no later amendment. On the face of that text the subdivision (b) window closed: an action filed on or after January 1, 2026 is governed by subdivision (a) alone.

A MISSPELLING IN THE ENACTED TEXT OF SENATE BILL 447, CORRECTED TWO YEARS LATER BY A CODE-MAINTENANCE BILL
The chaptered text of Senate Bill 447 (Stats. 2021, Ch. 448) contains a spelling defect in the section it enacted. In subdivision (d)(1) the chaptered bill directs the Judicial Council to report on "all judgements, consent judgements, or court-approved settlement agreements" — the non-standard spelling, twice, in enacted text. Subdivision (c) of the very same section, two paragraphs earlier, spells the same word correctly three times: "a judgment, consent judgment, or court-approved settlement agreement." The section as enacted was therefore internally inconsistent in its spelling of its own operative noun. The correction came in Assembly Bill 1754 of 2023, a bill whose title is "Maintenance of the codes"; section 18 of that bill re-enacted section 377.34 with "judgments, consent judgments" and made no other change to the section's substance. That is why the Legislative Counsel's history note for section 377.34 records an amendment in 2023 that altered nothing a litigant would notice. The current official code display carries the corrected spelling.

QUIROZ V. SEVENTH AVENUE CENTER: A SURVIVOR CLAIM IS NOT A WRONGFUL DEATH CLAIM
The survival statutes are frequently confused with the wrongful death statutes, and the two run in opposite directions. Quiroz v. Seventh Avenue Center states the distinction: unlike a cause of action for wrongful death, a survivor cause of action is not a new cause of action that vests in the heirs on the death of the decedent, but is instead a separate and distinct cause of action which belonged to the decedent before death but, by statute, survives that event. The practical consequence for a claim arising out of the separation of Maria Delgado is that the claim being prosecuted after death is the employee's own claim, brought in a representative capacity, measured by what the employee lost. A wrongful death claim, by contrast, belongs to the statutory heirs and compensates them for their own loss, and it exists only where the wrongful act caused the death. A termination is ordinarily not the cause of the death, so in the usual case there is a survivor claim and no wrongful death claim at all.

expectedJSON.body: Every other document in this corpus about the end of employment assumes that the former employee is alive to pursue whatever the separation left behind, and that the employer still exists to answer for it. This sheet describes what California statutes and published California opinions say happens when that assumption fails and a party dies while a termination-related claim is alive — a wrongful-termination action, a discrimination or retaliation claim, a suit for unpaid final wages, or an administrative matter that has become a lawsuit. The corpus already covers the money a deceased employee leaves behind: the affidavit procedure by which a surviving spouse collects a decedent's unpaid compensation without probate, the COBRA and Cal-COBRA qualifying event that the covered employee's death creates, and the group life insurance conversion privilege. It has not previously covered the claim itself. The sheet sets out the survival statutes in the Code of Civil Procedure (Chapter 4 of Title 3 of Part 2, "Effect of Death"): whether the cause of action is lost, who takes it, what must be filed to prosecute or continue it, how long there is to start it, what damages remain recoverable and what damages drop out, and the mirror-image rules that apply when it is the employer who dies. It states what the authorities say. It does not evaluate the position of Maria Delgado, of Luis Delgado, or of Northgate Components, Inc., and it does not say what any of them should do.

Code of Civil Procedure section 377.20 states the general rule of survival. Subdivision (a) provides that, except as otherwise provided by statute, a cause of action for or against a person is not lost by reason of the person's death, but survives subject to the applicable limitations period. Subdivision (b) adds that the section applies even where the loss or damage occurs simultaneously with, or after, the death of the person who would have been liable. Section 377.21 states the companion rule for a case already on file: a pending action or proceeding does not abate by the death of a party if the cause of action survives. The two sections sit in Article 2 of the chapter, headed "Survival and Continuation." Read together they set the default in California: death changes who prosecutes or defends a claim arising out of the end of employment of Maria Delgado, and it changes what damages are recoverable, but it does not by itself extinguish the claim or end the lawsuit.

In an action or proceeding by a decedent's personal representative or successor in interest on the decedent's cause of action, the damages recoverable are limited to the loss or damage that the decedent sustained or incurred before death, including any penalties or punitive or exemplary damages that the decedent would have been entitled to recover had the decedent lived, and do not include damages for pain, suffering, or disfigurement. expectedJSON.body: The survival statutes are frequently confused with the wrongful death statutes, and the two run in opposite directions. Quiroz v. Seventh Avenue Center states the distinction: unlike a cause of action for wrongful death, a survivor cause of action is not a new cause of action that vests in the heirs on the death of the decedent, but is instead a separate and distinct cause of action which belonged to the decedent before death but, by statute, survives that event. The practical consequence for a claim arising out of the separation of Maria Delgado is that the claim being prosecuted after death is the employee's own claim, brought in a representative capacity, measured by what the employee lost. A wrongful death claim, by contrast, belongs to the statutory heirs and compensates them for their own loss, and it exists only where the wrongful act caused the death. A termination is ordinarily not the cause of the death, so in the usual case there is a survivor claim and no wrongful death claim at all.

The survival statutes do not create a cause of action.

Section 377.40 provides that, subject to the Probate Code part governing creditor claims, a cause of action against a decedent that survives may be asserted against the decedent's personal representative or, to the extent provided by statute, against the decedent's successor in interest. Section 377.41 provides that on motion the court shall allow a pending action against the decedent that does not abate to be continued against the personal representative, except that the court may not permit continuation against the personal representative unless proof of compliance with the creditor-claim part is first made. The Probate Code supplies what must be complied with. Section 9351 provides that an action may not be commenced against a decedent's personal representative on a cause of action against the decedent unless a claim is first filed and rejected in whole or in part. Section 9370 governs an action already pending at the time of death: it may not be continued unless a claim is first filed, the claim is rejected in whole or in part, and within three months after notice of rejection is given the plaintiff applies for an order substituting the personal representative — the three-month condition applying only if the rejection notice says so — and no recovery is allowed against property in the estate unless proof of compliance is made.
